items.prompt: Why are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune made mostly of gas rather than rock like the inner planets?

options.label: They formed closer to the Sun where more raw material was available
options.feedback: They actually formed much farther from the Sun than the rocky planets, not closer; proximity isn't what gave them their bulk.

options.label: They formed beyond the frost line, where ice could freeze solid, giving them enough extra material to grow massive and pull in surrounding gas
options.feedback: Far from the young Sun's heat, ices as well as rock could condense into solid material, so planets forming out there had far more raw matter to build from, and once one grew massive enough its gravity pulled in the surrounding hydrogen and helium too.

options.label: Their strong magnetic fields attracted gas from across the solar system
options.feedback: A magnetic field can trap and channel charged particles, but it can't reach out and gather neutral gas from across the disk; gravity is what pulled the gas in.

options.label: They were originally rocky planets that later turned to gas
options.feedback: A solid planet doesn't convert into gas; the giants built up a gas-rich composition from the start by pulling in surrounding material, they didn't transform from something else.

items.ok_title: Cold enough for more to freeze
items.ok_line: More solid material out there meant room to grow gas-rich.
items.ko_title: Not location swapped, not magnetism, not transformation
items.ko_line: What mattered was how much solid material the cold outer disk offered.
items.exp_title: Enough ice to grow big enough for gas
items.exp_text: Beyond a certain distance from the young Sun, it was cold enough for ices, not just rock and metal, to condense into solid grains, so planets forming there had access to far more raw material than the inner planets ever did. A core built from that abundance grew massive enough that its gravity could then pull in and hold onto the surrounding hydrogen and helium gas, which is what turned it into a giant.

items.prompt: Why has Jupiter's Great Red Spot storm raged for centuries instead of dying out the way storms do on Earth?

options.label: It draws energy from Jupiter's rings, which Earth's storms don't have access to
options.feedback: Jupiter's rings are extremely thin and hold too little material to power anything; they aren't feeding the storm.

options.label: It is anchored in place by one of Jupiter's moons
options.feedback: No moon holds the storm in place; it drifts and changes shape on its own within the atmosphere.

options.label: Cold temperatures on Jupiter freeze the storm and prevent it from breaking up
options.feedback: Cold alone doesn't sustain a storm — a frozen storm would stop swirling rather than keep raging on.

options.label: There is no solid surface underneath to create the friction that breaks storms apart on Earth
options.feedback: On Earth, a storm eventually drags across mountains, coastlines and other surface features that create friction and drain its energy; Jupiter has no solid surface at all beneath its atmosphere for a storm to snag on.

items.ok_line: No ground means no friction to wear the storm down.
items.ko_title: Not rings, not a moon, not cold
items.ko_line: What keeps Earth's storms short-lived is missing on Jupiter.
items.exp_title: A storm with nothing to snag on
items.exp_text: A storm on Earth loses energy as it drags across mountains, coastlines and other surface features, and that friction is what eventually breaks it apart. Jupiter's atmosphere sits over no solid ground at all, just deeper and deeper layers of gas, so a storm there has nothing to catch against and drag on, letting it keep circulating instead of wearing down the way storms on solid worlds do.

items.prompt: Why does Saturn have rings made of countless icy chunks instead of one or more ordinary moons in that same space?

options.label: Any moon-sized body that close to Saturn would be torn apart by tidal forces before it could hold together
options.feedback: Close enough to a massive planet, its gravity pulls harder on the near side of an object than the far side, stretching it, and inside a certain distance that stretching force overwhelms an object's own gravity holding it together.

options.label: Saturn's magnetic field shatters any moon that drifts too close
options.feedback: A magnetic field affects charged particles, not the solid rock and ice a moon is made of; it isn't what's breaking anything apart.

options.label: The material never had enough time yet to form a moon
options.feedback: The rings and their region have existed for a very long stretch of Saturn's history; time alone isn't why a moon hasn't formed there.

options.label: Saturn's rings are the leftover exhaust from its formation, and they simply never cleared away
options.feedback: Being unswept leftover material doesn't explain why no moon has formed from it since; something specific has to be stopping the material from clumping.

items.ok_line: Too close for a moon to ever hold itself together.
items.ko_title: Not magnetism, not lack of time, not simple leftovers
items.ko_line: It's about gravity pulling harder on one side of an object than the other.
items.exp_title: Too close for gravity to keep a moon whole
items.exp_text: Very close to a massive planet, its gravity pulls noticeably harder on the near side of an orbiting object than the far side, stretching the object apart, and inside a certain distance that stretching overwhelms the object's own gravity holding it together. Material orbiting Saturn within that distance can never gather itself into a single moon, so it stays spread out as countless separate icy fragments circling as a ring instead.

items.prompt: Why do the gas giants have vastly more moons than the rocky planets do?

options.label: Their rings constantly break off pieces that become new moons
options.feedback: Ring material and moons are mostly separate populations; the rings aren't steadily manufacturing new moons.

options.label: They orbit closer to the asteroid belt, where more material is available to be pulled in
options.feedback: The gas giants, especially the outer two, orbit far beyond the asteroid belt, not closer to it than the rocky planets do.

options.label: Their far greater mass gives them much stronger gravity, and they formed within a broad, material-rich disk of their own
options.feedback: A gas giant's enormous mass gives it gravity strong enough to hold onto objects across a wide surrounding region, and each giant is thought to have formed with its own smaller disk of gas and dust, out of which many moons condensed directly.

options.label: They generate moons internally through volcanic activity
options.feedback: A planet's gravity doesn't manufacture moons out of nothing from inside itself; moons come from surrounding material captured or accreted from outside.

items.ok_line: Bigger gravity plus a leftover disk of their own.
items.ko_title: Not the rings, not proximity to the belt, not volcanoes
items.ko_line: It comes down to mass and what surrounded each giant while it formed.
items.exp_title: Strong gravity working with a disk of its own
items.exp_text: A gas giant's mass gives it gravity strong enough to reach out and capture objects across a wide surrounding region, far more than a small rocky planet ever could. Each giant is also thought to have formed with a miniature disk of gas and dust swirling around it, much like the Sun's own disk on a smaller scale, and many of its moons condensed directly out of that surrounding material rather than needing to be captured at all.

items.prompt: Why does Uranus spin almost completely on its side compared with the other planets?

options.label: Its extreme cold froze its axis into that position
options.feedback: Temperature doesn't lock a planet's axis into any particular angle; cold affects what state its surface materials are in, not which way it points.

options.label: A massive collision early in its history is thought to have knocked it over
options.feedback: Early in the solar system's history, while planets were still colliding with leftover debris, Uranus is thought to have been struck by one or more massive bodies with enough force to knock its spin axis over.

options.label: Its rings pull on it constantly, dragging its axis sideways over time
options.feedback: Uranus's rings are far too thin and low in mass to exert a meaningful pull on the whole planet's orientation.

options.label: It orbits the Sun sideways, which naturally tips its spin the same way
options.feedback: Uranus's orbital path around the Sun lies in the same general plane as the other planets; it's the planet's spin, not its path, that's tipped over.

items.ok_line: One violent hit early on, and the tilt stuck.
items.ko_title: Not cold, not rings, not its path
items.ko_line: Something struck the planet hard enough to tip its spin, long ago.
items.exp_title: A tilt frozen in place since a violent youth
items.exp_text: While the solar system was still young and full of debris left over from planet formation, Uranus is thought to have been struck by one or more large bodies with enough force to knock its spin axis far out of alignment with the other planets. Once a planet's axis is tipped that far, nothing in the quiet solar system since has had the force needed to tip it back.

items.prompt: Why does Neptune have the fastest winds of any planet despite receiving the least sunlight of the eight?

options.label: Its own internal heat, left over from formation, drives its atmosphere rather than sunlight
options.feedback: At Neptune's distance sunlight is far too weak to power its storms, so instead the internal heat it still radiates from its formation drives powerful convection through the atmosphere.

options.label: Its rings funnel gas into narrow, high-speed jets
options.feedback: Neptune's rings are far too faint and thin to funnel or accelerate any meaningful amount of atmospheric gas.

options.label: Its extremely fast rotation whips the atmosphere around by itself
options.feedback: Neptune's rotation rate is comparable to Jupiter's and Saturn's, not exceptionally fast, so spin rate alone doesn't set it apart as the windiest.

options.label: Sunlight reflecting off its moons adds extra energy to the atmosphere
options.feedback: Sunlight bouncing off small distant moons delivers far too little energy to meaningfully heat or move a planet-sized atmosphere.

items.ok_title: Its own furnace, not the Sun's
items.ok_line: Heat from inside, not sunlight from outside, drives the wind.
items.ko_title: Not rings, not spin, not reflected light
items.ko_line: The energy source here is inside the planet, not overhead.
items.exp_title: Powered from within, not from above
items.exp_text: Weather on most planets is driven mainly by heat absorbed from sunlight, but at Neptune's distance the sunlight arriving is far too weak to power much of anything. Neptune instead radiates a good deal of leftover heat from its own formation out into space, and that internal heat drives strong convection currents through its atmosphere, churning up winds despite the planet receiving barely any warmth from the Sun at all.

items.prompt: Why is there no solid ground anywhere inside a gas giant like Jupiter to land a spacecraft on?

options.label: The intense radiation there vaporizes any solid material instantly
options.feedback: Radiation levels, though strong in places, aren't what determines whether the interior has a solid surface; the makeup of the planet itself is.

options.label: A thick layer of clouds hides a rocky surface deep underneath
options.feedback: Going deeper doesn't lead to a hidden rocky floor; the gas simply keeps getting denser without ever turning into rock.

options.label: It's overwhelmingly hydrogen and helium that gradually gets denser with depth, turning to liquid and then a strange metallic state, without ever becoming a solid crust
options.feedback: Jupiter is built almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, and going deeper compresses that gas into a thick liquid layer, and deeper still into an exotic metallic form, with no sharp boundary anywhere that could be called solid ground.

options.label: Its rapid rotation flings any solid material out toward its rings
options.feedback: Rotation affects the planet's shape and weather patterns, not whether solid rock exists deep inside it; there's no rocky material being flung anywhere.

items.ok_title: Gas all the way down, changing form
items.ok_line: Denser and denser, but never turning to rock.
items.ko_title: Not radiation, not hidden rock, not spin
items.ko_line: The planet's whole makeup is gas, compressed but never solidified into a crust.
items.exp_text: Jupiter is built almost entirely from hydrogen and helium, and descending into the planet doesn't lead toward a rocky floor the way digging into Earth does. Increasing pressure gradually squeezes that gas into a thick liquid layer, and deeper still into a strange, electrically conductive metallic form, all without ever crossing a boundary that could be called a solid crust.

items.prompt: Why does Jupiter radiate more heat out into space than it actually receives from the Sun?

options.label: Its rings reflect extra sunlight back onto the planet
options.feedback: Jupiter's rings are extremely faint and reflect only a negligible amount of light; they aren't adding meaningful extra heat.

options.label: Nuclear reactions in its core, like a small star, generate the extra heat
options.feedback: Jupiter's core, however hot, has never come close to the pressure and temperature needed to sustain nuclear reactions; it isn't fusing anything.

options.label: Sunlight reflecting off its many moons adds extra warmth
options.feedback: Reflected light from distant moons delivers far too little energy to account for the heat Jupiter gives off.

options.label: Leftover heat from its formation, along with slow ongoing gravitational contraction, keeps generating warmth from within
options.feedback: When Jupiter formed, the collapse of gas under its own gravity generated an enormous amount of heat that is still slowly leaking out today, and the planet also keeps shrinking by a tiny amount as gravity compresses it further, converting more gravitational energy into heat.

items.ok_title: Heat from its own birth and squeeze
items.ok_line: Leftover formation heat, topped up by slow contraction.
items.ko_title: Not the rings, not fusion, not reflected moonlight
items.ko_line: The extra heat is generated by the planet itself, from inside.
items.exp_title: Still cooling down from its own birth
items.exp_text: When Jupiter first formed, the collapse of gas under its own gravity released an enormous amount of heat, and the planet has been slowly radiating that leftover warmth away ever since. It is also still very gradually contracting under its own gravity, and that ongoing squeeze converts a little more gravitational energy into heat all the time, adding to what remains from its formation and pushing its total output above what it receives from the distant Sun.

items.prompt: Why do Uranus and Neptune look blue-green while Jupiter and Saturn look yellow-brown?

options.label: Uranus and Neptune are much colder, and cold gas always looks blue
options.feedback: Temperature by itself doesn't dictate colour; plenty of cold gas is perfectly colourless. What matters here is which gas is present and what it does to light.

options.label: Methane in the upper atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune absorbs red light and lets blue light scatter back, while Jupiter and Saturn have far less methane
options.feedback: Methane absorbs red light strongly while leaving blue and green light largely untouched, so that unabsorbed light is what scatters back to an observer's eye; Jupiter and Saturn carry far less methane and instead reflect other tinting compounds.

options.label: Uranus and Neptune are covered in oceans of liquid water, which look blue from a distance
options.feedback: Any water these planets hold is buried deep beneath crushing layers of atmosphere, far too deep to be what's giving them their visible colour.

options.label: Sunlight arrives already tinted blue by the time it reaches such distant planets
options.feedback: Sunlight doesn't change colour as it travels through empty space; it reaches every planet with essentially the same mix of colours.

items.ok_title: A gas that eats red light
items.ok_line: Methane keeps the red; blue and green bounce back.
items.ko_title: Not temperature, not oceans, not tinted sunlight
items.ko_line: The colour comes from a specific gas absorbing part of the light.
items.exp_title: One gas absorbing, one gas reflecting
items.exp_text: Methane in the upper atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune absorbs red light strongly while leaving blue and green light largely untouched, so that unabsorbed light is what scatters back to reach an observer's eye. Jupiter and Saturn hold much less methane and instead carry clouds of ammonia and other compounds that reflect a different mix of colours, which is why they look yellow-brown rather than blue-green.

items.prompt: Why do gas giants like Jupiter generate such powerful magnetic fields despite having no solid iron core spinning inside them the way Earth does?

options.label: Their rings are made of magnetized ice that generates the field
options.feedback: Rings are far too thin and low in mass to generate a planet-wide magnetic field; the field comes from deep inside the planet, not from the rings.

options.label: Their rapid rotation alone is enough, with no need for anything conductive inside
options.feedback: Fast rotation by itself moves nothing that can generate a field; there has to be an electrically conductive material being stirred for rotation to matter.

options.label: Deep inside, immense pressure squeezes hydrogen into an electrically conductive metallic state, which fast rotation stirs into a dynamo
options.feedback: Deep inside a gas giant, extreme pressure squeezes hydrogen into a liquid metallic state that conducts electricity almost like a metal, and the planet's fast rotation stirs that conductive layer into a dynamo.

options.label: Sunlight reflecting off their cloud tops charges the outer atmosphere
options.feedback: Reflected sunlight doesn't charge a planet's atmosphere in any way that could generate a deep, planet-wide magnetic field.

items.ok_title: A metal-like layer, without any metal
items.ok_line: Squeezed hydrogen conducts electricity just as well.
items.ko_title: Not the rings, not spin alone, not reflected light
items.ko_line: It takes a conductive layer being stirred by rotation, whatever that layer is made of.
items.exp_title: A dynamo built from squeezed hydrogen
items.exp_text: Deep inside a gas giant, pressure becomes so extreme that hydrogen, ordinarily an insulator, is squeezed into a liquid state that conducts electricity almost like a metal. Fast rotation stirs that conductive layer, and a stirred, conductive fluid generates a magnetic field the same way a churning molten iron core does inside Earth, even though no iron or rock is involved at all.
